strengths: The paper targets a meaningful evaluation gap: multi-step spatial reasoning in MLLMs, beyond static spatial-relation VQA. The LEGO construction setting is intuitive and well matched to sequential 3D reasoning, with tasks spanning spatial understanding, single-step assembly reasoning, and multi-step reasoning.

The benchmark design is reasonably broad for a first dataset: 11 task types, balanced task counts, multiple-choice formats, and examples that probe height, adjacency, rotation, viewpoint, ordering, dependency, and outlier detection.

The experimental coverage is strong in terms of model breadth, with 20 MLLMs including major proprietary and open-source models, plus random and statistical random-baseline references. The human comparison also helps calibrate the difficulty of the benchmark.

The results reveal useful empirical findings: even strong proprietary models remain far below human performance, many open-source models are near random on several tasks, and chain-of-thought prompting provides inconsistent benefit for longer spatial sequences.

The exploratory generation evaluation is a nice extension showing that spatial understanding weaknesses also appear in image generation/editing settings, and the qualitative examples make the failure modes more concrete.
weaknesses: For a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution, the reproducibility case is not yet convincing. The first page shows “Project Page” and “Code”, but the PDF appears to contain no embedded links, and the manuscript does not provide concrete release details, dataset schema, source lists, annotation files, prompts, or scripts sufficient to reconstruct the benchmark.

The dataset is relatively small: 1,100 QA pairs total, with only 100 samples per task, and the additional Next-k-Step experiment uses only 20 cases per k. This limits statistical power, especially when drawing model-ranking and step-length conclusions across many models and tasks.

The data sourcing and licensing are under-specified. The paper says open-source LEGO source files were collected from the Internet, but does not identify sources, licenses, redistribution permissions, filtering criteria, or whether generated renderings and instructions can be safely released.

Quality control is described only at a high level. The paper mentions three trained annotators and disagreement resolution, but reports no inter-annotator agreement, rejection rates, duplicate thresholds, or audit examples. This is important because many tasks depend on subtle orientation, occlusion, and assembly-state distinctions.

The evaluation protocol has potential fragility. Rule-based answer extraction followed by ChatGPT-based matching can introduce unmeasured parsing bias; the paper does not report failure rates of the heuristic matcher, validation of the LLM matcher, or sensitivity to output formatting across models.

Several claims about generalization are stronger than the evidence supports. The comparison to 3DSRBench uses only proprietary models and only two aligned task types, so high Pearson correlations on this small set are not enough to establish that LEGO-Puzzles is a robust proxy for real-world spatial reasoning.

The benchmark may contain exploitable multiple-choice artifacts. The paper does not analyze option construction, answer distribution beyond random baselines, visual shortcuts, lexical cues, or whether models can solve questions from text-only prompts or image-only priors.

The image generation evaluation is interesting but thin: only 100 questions, 5 human raters, subjective 0–3 scores, and no reported rater agreement or rubric examples. As a result, it is better viewed as anecdotal exploratory evidence than a strong benchmark component.

The paper has noticeable writing and presentation issues, including repeated phrases, typos, awkward task wording, and some cluttered figures. These do not invalidate the idea, but they reduce clarity for a benchmark that depends on precise task definitions.

Overall, the benchmark idea is timely and potentially useful, but the current manuscript leaves important concerns about dataset release, provenance, scale, annotation reliability, and evaluation validity. I would lean slightly against acceptance unless these details are substantially strengthened.

strengths: The paper targets an important and under-evaluated capability: multi-step spatial reasoning in MLLMs. Using LEGO assembly as a controlled source of spatial transformations is intuitive, visually interpretable, and potentially scalable.

The benchmark is organized into a sensible progression from basic spatial understanding to single-step and multi-step sequential reasoning, with 11 task types that cover several distinct failure modes such as height, rotation, viewpoint, dependency, ordering, and outlier detection.

The empirical evaluation covers a broad set of 20 proprietary and open-source MLLMs, and the results show useful qualitative trends, especially the large gap between current models and humans and the weakness of many open-source systems on multi-step tasks.

The paper includes some useful additions beyond a standard multiple-choice benchmark, including human comparison, exploratory image-generation tasks, a Next-k-Step analysis, and a small comparison to 3DSRBench to argue that the synthetic setting captures some real-image spatial reasoning behavior.
weaknesses: As a Datasets/Benchmarks paper, the submission does not provide enough evidence that the dataset is reliable, representative, and reproducible. The manuscript says LEGO source files are collected from the Internet and rendered with Studio, but it does not sufficiently document the sources, licenses, filtering criteria, release format, or whether the benchmark/code/data will actually be usable by the community beyond placeholders for project page and code.

The dataset is quite small for the claims made: 1,100 VQA samples, 100 per task, and only 20 samples per task for the human comparison. Many conclusions are stated broadly, but the paper reports no confidence intervals, bootstrap estimates, statistical tests between models, or uncertainty analysis. With 100 examples per task and multiple-choice answers, several reported differences are likely not meaningful.

Annotation and quality control are underspecified. The paper mentions three trained annotators and removing unresolved disagreements, but gives no inter-annotator agreement, disagreement rate, number of discarded samples, annotator instructions, or examples of ambiguous cases. The human result of only 70% on the Height task suggests either substantial ambiguity or difficulty in the task construction, but this is not analyzed.

The benchmark design appears vulnerable to shortcutting and ambiguity. Many tasks are multiple choice with rendered LEGO images, but the paper does not analyze option bias, visual saliency shortcuts, color/shape priors, dependence across samples from the same LEGO projects, or possible memorization/contamination from public LEGO instruction manuals that may be in model training data.

Several experimental choices reduce reproducibility and rigor. Answer extraction uses VLMEvalKit plus ChatGPT-based matching when heuristics fail, but the exact prompts, model version, failure rate of rule matching, and validation of the matcher are not reported. The generation evaluation is also subjective, with only 100 prompts and 5 experts, but no rubric detail, agreement statistics, or examples of score calibration.

The Next-k-Step analysis is not convincing as evidence for multi-step degradation. It uses only 20 cases per k, and the results are noisy and sometimes contradict the narrative, e.g. Qwen2.5-VL-72B remains high or even improves at larger k. The paper still draws broad conclusions about step-wise degradation without adequate statistical support.

The novelty relative to existing synthetic spatial reasoning and 3D reasoning benchmarks is moderate. LEGO provides a nice visual domain, but the paper mainly repackages templated VQA over rendered assembly steps. The relationship to prior benchmarks such as CLEVR/Super-CLEVR/3DSRBench and what fundamentally new capability is isolated here is not established deeply enough.

The paper overclaims in places. Phrases such as “first benchmark explicitly designed to assess multi-step spatial reasoning” and “comprehensive evaluation” feel too strong given the small dataset, limited task instances, and the presence of related sequential/spatial reasoning evaluations. The discussion also claims generalization to natural images based on correlations over only two task types and proprietary models, which is too limited.

Presentation quality is below the expected bar. There are many typos and inconsistencies, including “seperated,” “there spatial,” “iamge,” “performace,” repeated words in Related Work, inconsistent Backward/Backwards naming, and awkward formatting in figures/tables. These do not alone determine the decision, but they reinforce the impression that the benchmark documentation and validation need more care.

The paper lacks a meaningful limitations and societal-impact discussion. For a benchmark intended to guide model development, it should discuss synthetic-to-real limitations, cultural/domain specificity of LEGO assemblies, accessibility of proprietary model evaluations, licensing constraints, and possible risks of over-optimizing to a small templated test set.

strengths: The paper makes a timely Datasets/Benchmarks contribution: LEGO-Puzzles targets multi-step spatial reasoning in MLLMs, a capability that is clearly important for vision-language systems and under-covered by existing benchmarks focused mainly on static spatial relations.

The task taxonomy is well motivated and progressively structured, covering spatial understanding, single-step assembly reasoning, and multi-step sequential reasoning across 11 tasks. The LEGO setting is a clever choice because it provides controllable 3D structure, stepwise transformations, and scalable generation from public assembly instructions.

The experimental coverage is strong for a benchmark paper: 20 MLLMs are evaluated, including both proprietary and open-source models, with random and statistical critical-value baselines, a human comparison subset, generation experiments, and an additional Next-k-Step analysis probing degradation with longer reasoning chains.

The findings are interesting and useful: even top models such as GPT-4o and Gemini-2.0-Flash remain far below human performance, and the breakdowns identify specific weaknesses in height, rotation, ordering, and long-range sequential reasoning.

The paper includes quality-control procedures with duplicate filtering, image-format checks, and multi-annotator validation, which supports the reliability of the benchmark. The planned release of project/code also improves potential reproducibility.
weaknesses: The benchmark size is somewhat modest: 1,100 VQA samples, apparently 100 per task, may be enough for diagnosis but limits statistical power and makes per-task rankings sensitive to sample selection. The paper would be stronger with confidence intervals, bootstrap tests, or more analysis of sample diversity and difficulty distribution.

The generalization claim beyond synthetic LEGO renderings is only partially supported. The Pearson correlation with 3DSRBench is computed for only two analogous tasks and only proprietary models, so the evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive.

Some evaluation details remain underspecified. The LLM-based answer matching may introduce ambiguity or bias; the paper does not report how often heuristic matching fails, whether LLM judgments were audited, or how invalid/free-form responses were handled.

The human study and generation evaluation need more methodological detail. The paper mentions 30 human experts and 5 experts for generation scoring, but does not report recruitment criteria, inter-rater agreement, scoring variance, or detailed rubrics.

Because the benchmark is multiple-choice, some tasks may be solvable through visual matching or elimination rather than genuine spatial reasoning. The paper discusses failures but provides limited analysis of possible shortcut artifacts or option-bias controls.

Reproducibility and dataset governance could be clearer. The benchmark is derived from public LEGO projects and rendered with Studio/PDF extraction tools, but licensing, attribution of source models, exact filtering criteria, and release format are not fully discussed.

The writing is generally understandable but has several polish issues and typos, and some figure/table text is cramped. These are not fatal, but they slightly reduce clarity for a benchmark intended to be widely reused.

strengths: The paper is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution: it introduces LEGO-Puzzles, a focused benchmark for spatial understanding and multi-step spatial reasoning in MLLMs. This framing is appropriate, and the paper’s value comes from task design, curation, and broad empirical evaluation rather than a new algorithm.

The benchmark targets an important gap in current multimodal evaluation: sequential spatial reasoning and assembly-style planning. The two-part design, with 11 elementary VQA tasks plus controllable Plan-k-Step tasks, gives a useful progression from basic 3D relations to long-horizon planning.

The empirical coverage is strong for a benchmark paper. The authors evaluate 29 MLLMs on the elementary set, include both proprietary and open-source models, report random and statistically above-random baselines, and add human comparisons. The results show clear and interpretable gaps between humans, frontier proprietary models, and open-source models.

The Planning set is a particularly interesting contribution. Varying k from 1 to 8 and reporting exact match, set match, and overlap ratio helps diagnose whether failures come from selecting the right intermediate states or ordering them correctly.

The paper goes beyond multiple-choice evaluation by studying image-generation-based planning and single-turn generative variants of elementary tasks. This is valuable because many real applications of visual spatial reasoning require producing visual instructions or intermediate states, not only selecting an answer.

The data construction pipeline is reasonably well documented: the paper describes sourcing LEGO projects, rendering, metadata extraction, template-based QA generation, duplicate filtering, manual checks, and multi-annotator validation. The appendix includes prompt templates and additional qualitative cases, which improves reproducibility.
weaknesses: The benchmark size is modest relative to the breadth of claims. The Elementary set has only 100 samples per task, the Plan-k-Step VQA evaluation uses 20 cases per k, and the generative planning experiment uses 50 cases. These sample sizes are useful for diagnosis but may be too small to robustly support strong claims about frontier model capabilities across the full diversity of LEGO assembly and spatial reasoning.

The data sourcing and licensing story is under-specified. The paper says projects are collected from open-source LEGO files on the Internet, but does not clearly document licenses, redistribution permissions, project-level filtering criteria, or whether the benchmark can be legally and fully released. This is an important issue for a Datasets/Benchmarks submission.

The construction of distractors and possible shortcut controls need more detail. Many tasks are multiple-choice, and distractors are generated by modifying colors, positions, orientations, or steps. The paper does not convincingly rule out artifacts such as answer distribution bias, visual salience differences, option-order bias, or distractors that are easier/harder in systematic ways unrelated to spatial reasoning.

The human evaluation is helpful but not fully rigorous. The elementary human baseline uses a 220-question Lite subset rather than the full benchmark, the Planning human baseline uses only five experts, and the appendix notes that some height errors disappear after reminding participants to pay closer attention. This makes the claimed human-model gap directionally plausible but less clean as a calibrated human-performance estimate.

The generative planning evaluation is not entirely convincing. Matching generated images to topology-expanded candidates with MSE can be brittle under rendering differences, viewpoint/crop/style changes, and non-identical but semantically correct outputs. The paper partly addresses this with human evaluation on separate single-turn tasks, but the core multi-turn generation accuracy still depends on an automatic metric whose validity is not deeply analyzed.

The correlation-to-real-world claim is too narrow. The paper reports high Pearson correlations with 3DSRBench on only two conceptually related tasks and only proprietary models. This is suggestive but insufficient to conclude that LEGO-Puzzles broadly generalizes to natural-image spatial reasoning.

The benchmark’s synthetic/rendered nature is a double-edged sword. It enables controlled ground truth and scalability, but the paper could more clearly discuss domain limitations, rendering biases, and the extent to which performance transfers to real assembly, robotics, or physical manipulation settings.

Some writing and presentation issues reduce polish: there are repeated typos such as “saptial,” “Backwrds,” and “performace,” and several claims are phrased more strongly than the evidence supports. These are not fatal, but a benchmark paper needs especially precise documentation.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: evaluating multi-step spatial reasoning in MLLMs beyond static image QA. The LEGO assembly setting is intuitive, visually controlled, and naturally supports increasing reasoning horizons.
The benchmark is organized into meaningful task groups, from elementary spatial understanding to single-step and multi-step planning, which makes the evaluation easy to interpret.
The paper evaluates a reasonably broad set of 29 proprietary and open-source MLLMs for the VQA portion, and includes some human baselines, random baselines, and partial-match metrics for planning.
The inclusion of image-generation planning tasks is a useful direction, since many real applications require producing visual intermediate states rather than only selecting multiple-choice answers.
weaknesses: Although the appropriate contribution type is Datasets/Benchmarks rather than Algorithms/General, the benchmark evidence is not strong enough for acceptance. The dataset is small for a benchmark paper: 1,100 elementary examples, 20 planning cases per horizon for VQA, and only 10 generation cases per horizon. This limits statistical reliability and makes the strong claims about frontier MLLM failure less convincing.

Novelty is limited relative to recent block-assembly, origami, 3D spatial reasoning, and procedural planning benchmarks. The paper argues that LEGO-Puzzles is harder and includes image generation, but does not sufficiently establish that the benchmark measures a fundamentally new capability rather than another synthetic assembly variant.

Dataset construction and quality control are under-specified. The sources of open LEGO projects, licensing, filtering criteria, annotation instructions, inter-annotator agreement, disagreement rates, and duplicate-removal thresholds are vague. This is especially problematic because ground truth for several spatial-understanding tasks is human annotated.

The evaluation may be vulnerable to data leakage or memorization. The benchmark is built from open-source LEGO projects and rendered building instructions, but the paper does not analyze whether proprietary or open models may have seen the same projects, images, or instructions during pretraining.

The human baselines are not sufficiently rigorous. The Elementary human evaluation uses only 20 questions per task, and the Planning human evaluation uses only five expert participants. The appendix even acknowledges that some height examples are ambiguous enough for human mistakes unless participants are reminded to inspect carefully, which weakens claims that failures reflect model reasoning rather than task ambiguity.

The generation evaluation is particularly weak. Full-stage generative planning is judged by matching generated images to topology-expanded candidates using MSE, but the paper does not define thresholds or justify pixel-space MSE as a valid correctness metric for images produced by different generative models. This could penalize style/rendering differences or miss semantic errors.

The claim that LEGO-Puzzles generalizes to real-world spatial reasoning is not well supported. The correlation analysis uses only two task correspondences and only proprietary models, so the high Pearson correlations are based on a very small sample and do not validate the broader benchmark.

Experimental reporting lacks confidence intervals, significance tests across models/tasks, numeric tables for the planning curves, and robustness checks for prompt sensitivity or option-order bias. For a benchmark paper, these omissions make it hard to judge reliability.

The paper overstates some conclusions. Statements such as models “fail completely” or that the benchmark reveals “critical limitations” are sometimes based on small generated-image subsets or exact-match metrics in highly constrained multiple-choice settings.

Reproducibility is uncertain despite the claimed project page/code. The manuscript does not provide enough detail about rendering settings, asset normalization, topology expansion, annotation protocols, or API/version settings for proprietary models to allow independent reproduction.

strengths: Although no contribution type is explicitly declared, the paper is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution rather than an Algorithms/General paper. Under that framing, it makes a timely and useful contribution: LEGO-Puzzles targets multi-step spatial reasoning and planning, an important capability for embodied AI, robotics, and multimodal assistants that is not well covered by many static-image VQA benchmarks.

The benchmark design is compelling and progressively structured. The Elementary set decomposes LEGO assembly reasoning into 11 interpretable tasks spanning spatial understanding, single-step reasoning, and multi-step reasoning, while the Planning set provides length-controlled k-step planning tasks that directly test degradation with horizon length.

The experimental coverage is broad. The paper evaluates 29 MLLMs, including proprietary and open-source models, and reports random and statistically-above-random baselines. The results reveal a clear and useful empirical picture: even strong models such as GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro remain well below human performance, and accuracy collapses as planning length increases.

The paper includes human baselines, including a 30-participant evaluation on LEGO-Puzzles-Lite and expert evaluation for planning/generation tasks. This makes the reported model failures more meaningful, since many tasks are demonstrably solvable by humans rather than simply being ill-posed.

The inclusion of generative planning is a distinctive strength. Evaluating whether models can generate intermediate assembly states, rather than only choose among options, makes the benchmark more relevant to real use cases such as visual instruction following and automated assembly assistance.

The paper provides useful analysis beyond headline accuracy, including exact match, set match, and overlap ratio for planning, qualitative failure cases, and an initial comparison with 3DSRBench showing that LEGO-Puzzles performance correlates with related real-image spatial reasoning tasks.
The manuscript is generally clear, with concrete task examples, prompt templates, data-curation description, and appendices that make the benchmark easier to understand and potentially reproduce.
weaknesses: The dataset scale is somewhat modest for a benchmark paper: the Elementary set has 100 samples per task, the Planning VQA set has 20 cases per k, and the full-stage generation experiment uses only 50 cases. The results are still informative, but confidence in fine-grained model rankings and per-task conclusions would benefit from larger test sets or uncertainty intervals.

The data provenance and release details need more precision. The paper states that open-source LEGO projects are collected from the Internet, but it should more clearly describe licensing, filtering criteria, train/test contamination risks, project deduplication, and whether all assets, metadata, code, prompts, and annotations will be released in a reproducible form.

The quality-control process is plausible but under-reported. Three annotators verify QA pairs, yet the paper does not provide inter-annotator agreement, disagreement rates, removal rates, or examples of corrected/removed samples. These details matter because some tasks, especially height and 3D adjacency from rendered views, can be visually ambiguous.

The automatic evaluation of image-generation planning relies on MSE matching to rendered topology-expanded candidates. This may be brittle to small rendering, alignment, crop, lighting, or stylistic differences and may not reliably distinguish spatial correctness from pixel similarity. The paper partially addresses image evaluation with human ratings elsewhere, but the central full-stage generation accuracy would be stronger with additional validation of the automatic metric.

The claimed connection to real-world spatial reasoning is promising but limited. The correlation analysis uses only two task correspondences and proprietary models; it does not fully establish that performance on LEGO renderings generalizes broadly to natural images, physical scenes, or robotic manipulation settings.

The human baselines are useful but uneven. Planning uses only five expert participants, and the paper reports perfect accuracy without much detail on participant expertise, time limits, interface, or whether participants had access to any aids. This does not undermine the model-gap conclusion, but it limits how precisely one can interpret the human-model comparison.

Some tasks may reward recognition of rendered instruction artifacts or option elimination rather than pure spatial reasoning, especially in multiple-choice settings with synthetic distractors. More analysis of distractor construction, shortcut prevention, and robustness to prompt/option perturbations would strengthen the benchmark’s validity.

The manuscript has a number of presentation issues and typos, such as “cruical,” “saptial,” “Backwrds,” “perform poor,” and some awkward phrasing. These are not scientifically fatal, but polishing is needed for a camera-ready version.
